doc: Turning an upstream bus-stop or route-endpoint NAME into something a person reads. HK operators publish English names in ALL CAPS with the operator's own pole code bolted on in brackets — "CITY ONE STATION (ST311)" — and publish the Chinese name of the same pole with no code and no case at all. Four rules cover it: split the trailing code off so the UI can mute it, title-case the remainder without mangling romanised Cantonese, and detect/strip the loop marker HK circular routes carry inside their destination name (ADR-046). Every rule takes a NAME, never an id: nothing here may be pointed at a `stopId` or `routeId`, which have their own grammar in `src/ids.ts` (ADR-059). The rules are heuristics over a source that has no metadata to appeal to, so the rows below are the specification — a port that disagrees with one of them is wrong even if its own logic looks more principled.

splitStopCode.doc: Peel a trailing parenthesised operator code off a display name. `code` is JSON null when the name carries none, in which case `label` is the input verbatim — including any whitespace, because nothing was split so nothing is trimmed.

cases.name: city-one-station-splits-operator-code
cases.why: The canonical KMB shape, and the reason the rule exists: the pole code is data for the operator, not for the passenger, so the UI needs it as a separate field it can mute rather than as eight characters of shouting at the end of the name.

cases.name: tolerates-whitespace-after-the-code
cases.why: Upstream names arrive with trailing spaces. If the anchor were a bare `\)$` the code would go unsplit and the whole string would render as one label, so the trailing-space tolerance is load-bearing rather than defensive.

cases.name: no-trailing-code-returns-the-whole-name
cases.why: Citybus and GMB names usually have no pole code at all. The absent value must be absent, not an empty string: the UI renders the code slot only when it is present, and "" would paint an empty muted gap after every Citybus stop.

cases.name: mid-name-parenthetical-is-not-a-code
cases.why: A parenthetical that is part of the name must survive. Anchoring at the end is what separates "(ST311)" from a real disambiguator, and HK is full of the latter.

cases.name: real-mid-name-parenthetical-survives
cases.why: The live version of the row above: HK genuinely names stops "(SOUTH)" / "(NORTH)" to tell two poles apart. Losing that word would leave two different stops rendering under identical labels — the failure is silent and it is the one passengers act on.

cases.name: last-parenthetical-wins-when-there-are-two
cases.why: A disambiguator AND a pole code in the same name. The match is greedy on the label, so the code is the LAST bracketed group and the disambiguator stays in the label. A lazy quantifier would split at the first bracket and hand the UI "KAI TAK" plus a code of "MTR".

cases.name: letters-only-venue-code-is-still-a-code
cases.why: The code slot is positional, not shaped: a venue acronym with no digits splits exactly like "ST311". This is why `titleCaseName` needs its own KEEP_UPPER allowlist rather than a rule about brackets — by the time the text reaches it, the brackets are gone.

cases.name: full-width-brackets-are-not-a-code
cases.why: Pins an asymmetry that is easy to 'fix' by accident: this rule understands ASCII parentheses only, while `stripCircular` accepts full-width ones too. Chinese names are published with the loop marker in （）but never with a pole code, so widening the bracket class here would only ever produce a false split.

cases.name: empty-name
cases.why: An empty upstream name must not become an exception on the render path. A missing name is a data problem to show plainly, not a crash between the passenger and the ETA.

cases.name: whitespace-only-name-is-not-trimmed
cases.why: Nothing split, so nothing is trimmed — the label is the input byte for byte. Trimming here would be a quiet second responsibility, and it is `stripCircular`, not this rule, that owns whitespace.

titleCaseName.doc: Title-case an ALL-CAPS English name. Anything already containing a lower-case letter, or containing no Latin letters at all, is returned untouched — the rule only ever de-shouts, it never re-cases text somebody has already cased.

cases.name: all-caps-english-title-cases
cases.why: The base case. ALL CAPS is how KMB publishes, and a list of shouting stop names is the single loudest thing on the nearby screen.

cases.name: known-acronym-stays-upper-leading
cases.why: "Mtr Kowloon Station" is the giveaway that a title-caser was applied without an allowlist. Leading position, so this row also pins that an acronym is checked before the first-word rule.

cases.name: known-acronym-stays-upper-operator-name
cases.why: An operator initialism in a depot name. Same rule, different word — the allowlist is a set, and a port that special-cased only "MTR" would pass the row above and fail this one.

cases.name: known-acronym-stays-upper-trailing
cases.why: PTI (public transport interchange) at the END of the name. Covers the allowlist hit in non-first position, which is a different branch from the leading acronym above.

cases.name: minor-word-lower-cased-mid-title
cases.why: "Of" mid-title reads as a typo. This is the rule that forces a small-words set to exist at all.

cases.name: minor-word-for-lower-cased-mid-title
cases.why: A second member of the small-words set, so the set is pinned rather than one entry of it.

args.name: HONG KONG ACADEMY FOR PERFORMING ARTS

cases.expect: Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts

cases.name: on-is-a-romanised-syllable-lok-on-pai
cases.why: THE REASON THIS MODULE HAS A TEST. "On" in a HK place name is the romanised syllable 安, not the English preposition. Put "on" in the small-words set and Lok On Pai becomes "Lok on Pai" — wrong in a way that looks deliberate, across hundreds of stops.

cases.name: on-is-a-romanised-syllable-tsz-on-court
cases.why: Same syllable, different estate. Kept as a separate row because the temptation to add "on" to the small-words set recurs, and one example is easy to read as a quirk.

cases.name: on-is-a-romanised-syllable-hing-on-street
cases.why: The street-name form, where "on" is most likely to be mistaken for a preposition by a general-purpose title-caser trained on English prose.

cases.name: leading-syllable-on-is-capitalised
cases.why: First word is never minor. Pins that the first-word rule and the syllable rule agree rather than fighting.

cases.name: leading-minor-word-is-capitalised
cases.why: "the Peak" is the visible cost of applying the small-words set to position zero. This row is the whole justification for tracking `wasFirst`.

cases.name: already-mixed-case-is-left-alone
cases.why: Citybus and GMB publish names already cased. Re-casing them would re-shout an acronym the operator got right, and would make the same pole render differently depending on which operator's copy of it we read.

cases.name: cjk-name-is-left-alone
cases.why: No Latin letters means nothing to case. Chinese has no case, so any transformation here is damage; this is the guard that makes the whole module safe to call unconditionally on the active locale's name.

cases.name: latin-acronym-inside-a-chinese-name
cases.why: A Chinese name containing Latin capitals DOES pass the guard (it has A–Z, no a–z), so it runs the word pass. The row proves the CJK characters survive untouched and the acronym stays upper — the word regex matches Latin runs only.

cases.name: mixed-script-with-lower-case-is-left-alone
cases.why: The other half of the row above: one lower-case Latin letter anywhere means somebody already cased this string, so the whole thing is left alone rather than half-processed.

cases.name: apostrophe-stays-inside-the-word
cases.why: "St John'S" is what you get when the apostrophe ends the word and the next letter counts as a new one. The apostrophe is part of the word, not a separator.

cases.name: typographic-apostrophe-stays-inside-the-word
cases.why: Upstream mixes the ASCII apostrophe with the typographic one (’). Same rule, and a port whose word pattern only knows U+0027 renders "King’S Park".

cases.name: digits-and-punctuation-are-not-words
cases.why: A stop name carrying a route-ish number and a bracketed disambiguator. Numbers pass through untouched and the bracket does not start a new title, so the word after it is not treated as first.

cases.name: empty-name
cases.why: No upper-case letter, so the guard returns immediately. Same contract as `splitStopCode`: an empty upstream name renders as nothing, it does not throw on the way to the screen.

isCircular.doc: Does a route destination name carry the circular-route marker? A case-insensitive substring test over the three spellings HK operators use — "CIRCULAR", 循環 and 循环 — deliberately NOT anchored to the brackets, so a name that is marked in an unexpected way still answers true.

cases.name: english-circular-marker
cases.why: The English form. HK circular routes have no separate flag in the open data (ADR-046) — the loop lives in the destination string — so this substring test is the only signal there is.

cases.name: traditional-chinese-loop-marker
cases.why: 循環線 in the zh-Hant name. Detecting only the English form would make the same route circular in one locale and not the other, which is the class of drift this repo treats as a defect.

cases.name: simplified-chinese-loop-marker
cases.why: 循环线 in the zh-Hans name. 環 and 环 are different code points; matching one is not matching the other, and no normalization step runs before this.

cases.name: title-case-marker-matches
cases.why: Operators are not consistent about case. The test is case-insensitive so a name that has already been through `titleCaseName` still answers the same — order of operations on the render path must not change the answer.

cases.name: plain-destination-is-not-circular
cases.why: The negative case. A false positive here promotes an ordinary route to the 'Circular via …' treatment and hides its real destination.

cases.name: unbracketed-marker-still-counts
cases.why: Pins the deliberate asymmetry with `stripCircular`: detection is a substring test, stripping is anchored to a bracketed suffix. So this name is circular AND survives stripping intact — the UI shows the loop treatment without silently losing the word.

cases.name: empty-name
cases.why: A blank `en` is real in this dataset — ADR-060 keeps a row for a circular route whose English name is empty — so the blank must answer false rather than reach a substring index that does not exist.

stripCircular.doc: Remove a TRAILING bracketed loop marker and trim. Anchored to the end and to a bracket pair (ASCII or full-width) — anything else is left alone, because the marker is a suffix the operator appended, not a word we are entitled to delete from the middle of a place name.

cases.name: strips-english-marker
cases.why: The base case. The UI renders the loop as its own 'Circular via …' treatment, so leaving the raw suffix in place would say it twice.

cases.name: strips-title-case-marker
cases.why: Case-insensitive, so stripping works either side of `titleCaseName`. Both orders occur on the route screen.

cases.name: strips-traditional-marker-in-full-width-brackets
cases.why: The published zh-Hant form: full-width brackets around 循環線. A port that only knows ASCII parentheses leaves Chinese destinations with the suffix while English ones lose it.

cases.name: strips-simplified-marker-in-full-width-brackets
cases.why: 循环线, the zh-Hans spelling. Separate row from the traditional one because the characters differ, not the shape.

cases.name: strips-chinese-marker-in-half-width-brackets
cases.why: The same Chinese name with ASCII brackets — upstream mixes them within one feed. Bracket width and marker script vary independently, so both combinations have to be pinned.

cases.name: leaves-a-plain-destination-alone
cases.why: No marker, no change. The route screen calls this unconditionally, so a rule that mangled ordinary destinations would damage every non-circular route.

cases.name: only-a-trailing-marker-is-stripped
cases.why: A marker followed by more name is part of the name. Dropping it would turn 'circular via Mong Kok' into a destination that reads as a different terminus.

args.name: TAI KOK TSUI (CIRCULAR) VIA MONG KOK

cases.expect: TAI KOK TSUI (CIRCULAR) VIA MONG KOK

cases.name: unbracketed-marker-is-kept
cases.why: The pair to `isCircular`'s row of the same shape: the word is detected but not stripped, because stripping it would leave an empty destination. Losing the whole label is worse than showing a redundant one.

cases.name: trims-whitespace-around-the-result
cases.why: Upstream pads names. The trim runs after the substitution so the leading space goes too, and the label does not render with an inherited indent next to a route chip.

cases.name: whitespace-only-name-becomes-empty
cases.why: The trim applies even when nothing matched — unlike `splitStopCode`, which returns its input verbatim. Two rules, two whitespace contracts, and the difference is visible only in a row like this one.

cases.name: empty-name
cases.why: Blank in, blank out. Pairs with `isCircular`'s empty row so the blank-`en` route (ADR-060) has a defined answer from both halves of the pair.

poleNameKey.doc: A pole name folded to what a rider could actually see a difference in — case, spaces (including the ideographic U+3000), and the ASCII/CJK punctuation pairs the feed mixes. COMPARED, NEVER DISPLAYED. It exists because the difference between two names is the honest way to tell two identically-headed poles apart (WP5-12), and a byte comparison would ship a lie: measured over build `ceb33eed99461e04`, 21 colliding heading groups have names that differ ONLY by case or punctuation, so a byte test calls them distinct, the screen prints the same words twice, and the app claims the ambiguity has been resolved. The character list is explicit rather than `NFKC` on purpose: NFKC would make the hand-port depend on a whole Unicode table agreeing across three languages, while this list is inspectable and pinnable here.

cases.name: an-unchanged-name-folds-to-itself-lower-cased
cases.why: THE CONTROL. A fold that stripped too much would satisfy every equality row below while making two genuinely different names equal, which is the failure that matters — it prints "we cannot tell these apart" at a place where the wire says otherwise.

cases.name: a-case-only-difference-folds-equal
cases.why: Bonham Road, near Hospital Road — verbatim from build ceb33eed99461e04, where the two minibus poles 9.1 m apart differ by exactly one comma. This is the pair the required boundary row in `stop-detail#poleDistinctions` is built from.

cases.name: the-comma-form-of-the-same-name-folds-to-the-same-key
cases.why: The other half of the pair above. Two rows rather than one because the key is only useful as a comparison and a single row cannot state an equality.

cases.name: an-all-caps-name-folds-to-the-title-cased-one
cases.why: `KENT ROAD, near Kowloon Tong Station` and `Kent Road, near Kowloon Tong Station` are one place's two poles in this build. `titleCaseName` leaves an already-mixed-case name alone, so the printed strings really do differ.

args.label: KENT ROAD, near Kowloon Tong Station

cases.name: a-full-width-comma-folds-like-an-ascii-one
cases.why: The Chinese half of the same problem: `昭信路, 近煜明苑煒明閣` versus `昭信路，近煜明苑煒明閣`. A fold that handled only ASCII punctuation would be right in `en` and wrong in both Chinese locales, which is the shape of defect the second renderer exists to catch.

args.label: 昭信路，近煜明苑煒明閣

cases.expect: 昭信路近煜明苑煒明閣

cases.name: an-ideographic-space-and-a-dash-are-both-invisible
cases.why: Verbatim shapes from this build: `楊屋道,　近　荃灣公園` carries U+3000, and upstream uses `-`, `‐`, `–` and `—` interchangeably. Both are in the list; a reader should be able to check that against this row.

args.label: 楊屋道,　近　荃灣公園

poleFlagCode.doc: The operator's own flag code for a pole, in the locale a heading is printed in — BORROWING one from another locale when this one has none and the other's is flag-shaped (WP5-12). The borrow answers the lead WP5-12's row named: at Prince Edward Station two KMB poles sit at the same coordinate and read `PRINCE EDWARD STATION, MONG KOK POLICE STATION` in English while the Chinese carries `(MK356)` and `(MK357)`, so the code that tells them apart is on the wire and only the English label lacks it. A code is Latin letters and digits — what is printed on the physical flag — so it is locale-neutral by construction and showing the Chinese one to an English reader is the same string rather than a translation. The ACTIVE locale's own parenthetical is used verbatim whatever its shape, which is the pre-WP5-12 behaviour preserved; only the borrow is gated on the shape. Measured over build `ceb33eed99461e04`: of 63 poles whose `en` lacks a code while a Chinese name has one, 51 are flag-shaped and 12 are not, and 167 poles carry trailing parentheticals that DISAGREE across locales because they are translated place phrases.

cases.name: the-active-locales-own-code-wins
cases.why: THE CONTROL, and it is the pre-WP5-12 behaviour: when the printed name carries a code, that is the code, and nothing is borrowed. A rule that preferred another locale's would rewrite what a rider reads on 6 187 poles for no reason.

cases.name: an-english-name-with-no-code-borrows-the-chinese-one
cases.why: Prince Edward Station, verbatim. The two poles are at the SAME coordinate, so no compass rule can ever separate them and no fold may merge them (they are two real kerbs); the code is the only thing that can, and it was being thrown away because the English label lacks it.

name.en: PRINCE EDWARD STATION, MONG KOK POLICE STATION

cases.name: a-chinese-reader-of-the-same-pole-still-reads-its-own-code
cases.why: The borrow is not a rewrite: the active locale's parenthetical is preferred, so this returns the same string by the first rule rather than by the borrow. Both rows are needed — either alone passes an implementation that always searched every locale.

name.en: PRINCE EDWARD STATION, MONG KOK POLICE STATION

cases.name: a-translated-parenthetical-is-not-borrowed
cases.why: THE SECOND CONTROL, and the row that stops the borrow becoming a bug. `黃泥涌道55-57號(近翠景樓)` ends in a Chinese place phrase, not a code — 12 of the 63 candidates in this build are this shape — and borrowing it would put Chinese into an English heading. The shape gate (Latin letters then digits) is exactly the discriminator.

name.en: Wong Nai Chung Road No. 55-57 Green View Mansion

cases.name: no-code-in-any-locale-is-no-code
cases.why: THE THIRD CONTROL: the ordinary case for most of the network. A rule that invented something here would put a cue on every pole in Hong Kong.
